It pushes the boundaries of how much external reality a romance novel can handle before the central relationship fractures under the pressure.
It asks a lot of the reader's capacity to compartmentalize. But perhaps that extreme pressure, that impossible legal and financial weight,
is exactly what makes the final choice so potent. We've spent this entire time looking at Julia's trust fall. We've analyzed her Midwestern caution,

her Shakespearean armor, her terror of hitting the concrete after Will dropped her. We thought the title Trust Fall was about the Nebraska girl trusting the New York boy not to break her heart. But if you look closely at
the mechanics of the story, the ultimate trust fall wasn't hers. It was Damian's.
He had to fall completely away from his family's toxic empire, his limitless inheritance, and his rigidly predetermined Ivy League identity.
He had to step off the precipice of his entire known universe, trusting that Julia's world, the messy, unpolished Nebraska reality,
would be strong enough to catch him. The true risk wasn't her losing her heart.
The true risk was him losing his entire world just to find it.
